summary: This program defines a RobotPet class with a can_walk method that compares the pet's battery level against the energy a walk would need, then checks the method's behaviour with two assert statements. If both checks hold, the program prints a success message.

lines.text: The constructor runs whenever a new RobotPet is created and receives the three values that describe the pet.
Stores the battery level on the object so that can_walk can consult it later.
Defines the behaviour under test: given a walk length in minutes, decide whether this pet has the energy for it.

lines.code: """Check if the pet has enough energy for a walk of given duration (in minutes)."""
lines.text: A docstring records the method's contract in the code itself, so anyone reading or testing it knows what the units are.
Fixes the rule that every minute of walking costs two units of battery, giving the test a predictable number to work with.
Returns True or False by comparing the stored battery to the cost, which is exactly the value the asserts examine.
Creates a well-charged pet that should pass the walk check, setting up the positive test case.
Creates a pet with too little battery for a 30-minute walk, setting up the negative test case.

lines.code: assert rover.can_walk(30) == True, "Rover should be able to walk for 30 minutes"
lines.text: An assert states a fact that must hold; 85 battery beats the 60 required, so the program continues silently. The text after the comma is the message shown if the fact ever stops being true.

lines.code: assert beep.can_walk(30) == False, "Beep should not be able to walk for 30 minutes"
lines.text: Tests the other side of the rule: 45 battery is below the 60 needed, so can_walk must say no. Good tests check failures as well as successes.
Because a failed assert stops the program immediately, reaching this line is proof that both checks held.
